(InStyle.com) -- As an aspiring young ballerina, 9-year-old Brooke Burns adopted a decidedly bold approach to cosmetics. "I would borrow my mom's red Borghese lipstick and smear it on like a clown!" she recalls. "For sexy eyes, there is nothing better than this drugstore black liner." Today, the 29-year-old Burns—now a single mother—strives to impart more refined application techniques to her 7-year-old daughter. "I taught her 'a dab'll do ya,'" says the actress, who stars in the ABC comedy *Miss Guided*. "She's going to wear it anyway, so she might as well have some experience."

**Did you pick up any makeup tricks working as a model?**
One of my favorites is applying white pencil to the inside of the lower eyelid for a wonderfully bright, wide-awake look. In the evening, when I'm pressed for time, I'll simply layer on plenty of mascara and trace black pencil all the way around the inner rim. It creates a thoroughly sexy eye in about a minute and a half.

**What's the one makeup item you can't live without?**
I'm absolutely in love with Revlon ColorStay foundation. I can do anything while wearing it, and it never budges. What's more, it contains sunscreen, lends me a beautifully natural glow, and covers everything.

**You alternate between being a blonde and a brunette. Which do you prefer?**
My natural color is dark blond, but at the moment I'm enjoying being a brunette. I filmed a movie last summer for which they dyed my hair platinum—and I absolutely hated it. I have a big personality, and I find that a big personality paired with blond hair can make me come across as rather glib. With dark hair, people focus more on your face; before, it was all about the hair.

**How do you keep color-treated hair healthy?**
I've never found a conditioner that leaves my hair feeling as remarkable as Nature's Therapy Mega Moisture Nurturing shampoo by L'Oréal. My hairdresser used it on me once, and now I'm completely obsessed. I also use a new color from Paul Mitchell—it's called Fudge Brownie—that's simply incredible. So many people remark, "Your hair looks so healthy!"

**Have you always had great hair?**
No, not at all. I had seriously big hair in high school. I was a devoted user of hot rollers and teasing, and I sported mall bangs. I also wore my hair in a bun quite often because of all the dancing I did. I really wasn't very popular in high school.

**No one will believe you if you say you weren't popular.**
"Olive Oyl" was my nickname. I was utterly gangly and stood a foot taller than all the boys. It was not an attractive look.

**Clearly you've come a long way. What's your secret?**
I believe it's tremendously important to take care of your skin, and the number-one priority is, of course, sunscreen. All my life I've used Oil of Olay as my daytime moisturizer, because my mom did. I also use their foaming face wash—it's the finest makeup remover ever. And in the morning I use Olay Age Defying Daily Renewal cleanser, because it contains tiny microbeads that are wonderful for exfoliating. People say, "You have such great skin!" and I think, "Thank goodness I'm not spending $150 on products." I'm sure those products are excellent, but if it ain't broke, don't fix it.

# Brooke Burns on Beauty and Style

As a child, Brooke Burns approached makeup with a heavy hand, applying it dramatically the way many young girls first experiment with cosmetics. Today, she takes a different approach with her own daughter, teaching her more subtle techniques. Rather than discouraging early makeup use altogether, Burns embraces the philosophy that gaining experience with beauty products from a young age is genuinely valuable.

Throughout her career, Burns picked up a number of professional makeup tricks from her time in modeling. Among her favorites is using a white pencil on the inner eyelid to create a bright, awake appearance. She also relies on a black pencil applied around the inner rim of the eye for a quick, sultry look that instantly adds a touch of sexiness.

When it comes to her must-have product, Burns points to Revlon Color Stay foundation. She values it for its long-lasting coverage, the built-in sunscreen that protects her skin, and the natural glow it lends to her complexion.

Burns also has clear preferences when it comes to her hair color. She favors being a brunette over blond, explaining that dark hair draws attention to her face rather than making her appear glib. For her, the richer color feels more flattering and true to who she is.

Maintaining color-treated hair requires special care, and Burns has found a routine that works. She depends on L'Oréal's Nature's Therapy Mega Moisture shampoo along with Paul Mitchell's Fudge Brownie color to keep her locks in top condition. The results speak for themselves—others frequently compliment her on how healthy her hair looks.

# Beauty, Naturally: A Conversation with Brooke Burns

Actress and former model Brooke Burns has spent years in front of the camera, and along the way she's learned a thing or two about looking her best. But sit down with the single mom for an honest conversation, and you'll quickly discover that her approach to beauty is refreshingly grounded—rooted in lessons from her childhood and refined during her days on the runway and in photo studios.

"My philosophy is pretty simple," Brooke explains. "Beauty should feel effortless, even when a little effort goes into it. I've never been someone who wants to hide behind a full face of makeup. I want to look like myself, just a bit more polished and awake."

## Lessons That Stuck

Some of Brooke's most treasured tips date back to her early years. "My mom and the women in my family taught me the basics before I ever set foot in front of a professional makeup artist," she says. "Little things—like taking care of your skin first, drinking plenty of water, never going to bed with your makeup on. Those habits matter more than any product."

Her modeling career filled in the rest of her education. Working with top artists on shoots, she picked up professional secrets that she still relies on today. "You learn so much just by watching. The pros know how to enhance features rather than mask them, and that's stayed with me."

## Her Go-To Products and Tricks

When it comes to specifics, Brooke is happy to share what works for her. One of her favorite tricks? Reaching for a white eye pencil. "If you line the inner rims of your eyes with a white pencil, it instantly makes you look more awake and rested—even on the mornings when you're anything but," she laughs. "It's the perfect fix for a tired mom who's been up half the night."

For her base, she keeps things reliable. "I love Revlon Color Stay foundation," she says. "It really does stay put, which is exactly what I need when I'm running around all day. I don't want to be worrying about touch-ups or my makeup sliding off."

Her overall routine reflects the same practical mindset—a good foundation, a few strategic touches to brighten the eyes, and minimal fuss.

## A New Look, A New Perception

Perhaps the biggest change in Brooke's beauty story came not from a product, but from a bold decision: swapping her signature blonde locks for a richer brunette shade.

"It's amazing how differently people treat you," she reflects. "As a blonde, I think people made certain assumptions—maybe they saw me as softer, or more of a 'girl next door.' Once I went brunette, people started perceiving me as more serious, more sophisticated. Even my personality reads differently to them."

The transformation, she notes, was as much about self-discovery as it was about appearance. "The hair changed how the world saw me, but honestly, it also changed how I saw myself. I felt like a slightly different version of me—and I really liked her."

For Brooke Burns, beauty isn't about chasing trends or hiding flaws. It's about feeling confident, staying true to herself, and holding onto the wisdom she's gathered along the way—one white pencil trick at a time.

# In Conversation with Brooke Burns: The Actress on Effortless Beauty, Golden Hues, and Aging Gracefully

*The former "Baywatch" star and beloved TV host opens up about her no-fuss approach to beauty, why she embraces her natural hair color, and the skincare philosophy that keeps her glowing.*

---

There's an easy warmth to Brooke Burns when she settles into her chair, fresh-faced and radiant in natural light. The actress and television personality—known for her breezy California-girl charm—has never been one to overcomplicate beauty. "I've learned that less is truly more," she tells *InStyle*, tucking a strand of golden hair behind her ear. "The older I get, the more I want to look like myself, just well-rested."

We sat down with Burns to talk everything from her five-minute makeup routine to the skincare products she can't live without.

---

**InStyle: Let's start with makeup. What does your everyday look consist of?**

**Brooke Burns:** Honestly? It's minimal. I'm a mom, I'm busy, and I don't have an hour to sit in front of a mirror. My go-to is a good tinted moisturizer or a light foundation with SPF built in—I never skip sun protection. Then I'll do a cream blush, because it looks so natural and dewy, a swipe of mascara, and a nude or berry lip depending on my mood. That's really it for daytime.

**Any tips for people who want that "your skin but better" glow?**

Cream products, cream products, cream products! Powders can look flat and can age you. A cream blush and a little cream highlighter on the tops of your cheekbones give you that lit-from-within look. And I always blend with my fingers—the warmth helps everything melt into the skin.

**What about for evening or a red carpet?**

That's when I have fun with it. I love a smoky eye in warm bronzes and coppers—they bring out my eyes. I'll add a little more definition to my brows and maybe a bold lip. But I still keep the skin looking fresh rather than heavily contoured. I want people to see *me*, not a mask.

---

**Your hair color is such a signature. Tell us about it.**

I've embraced my golden blonde, but I keep it looking natural with dimension. I'm not a fan of the solid, one-note blonde—it can look brassy and flat. I ask my colorist for soft, sun-kissed highlights, like I've spent a week at the beach. Lowlights are just as important because they add depth and make the blonde look more expensive.

**How do you keep blonde hair healthy?**

Blonde can get so dry, so I'm religious about hydrating masks—once a week, minimum. I use a purple shampoo to keep the tone from going brassy, but only every few washes because it can be drying if you overdo it. And I try not to wash my hair every day. Dry shampoo is my best friend for stretching out styles and keeping some natural oils in.

**Any heat-styling secrets?**

Always use a heat protectant—non-negotiable. And I've fallen in love with air-drying when I can. I'll scrunch in a little texturizing cream and let my natural wave do its thing. It's so freeing to not fight your hair's natural texture.

---

**Now let's talk skincare, because your complexion is glowing. What's your routine?**

Skincare is where I invest my time and money—makeup is just the finishing touch. In the morning, I cleanse gently, use a vitamin C serum for brightness and protection, moisturize, and then the most important step: sunscreen. I cannot stress SPF enough. It's the single best thing you can do for your skin.

**And at night?**

At night I double cleanse if I've been wearing makeup, then I use a retinol a few nights a week—it's been a game changer for texture and fine lines. On the off nights I use a hydrating serum with hyaluronic acid. I finish with a rich moisturizer and eye cream. I've also become a big believer in facial oils; a few drops give my skin that dewy bounce.

**Any lifestyle habits that contribute to your skin?**

Water, sleep, and managing stress. I know it sounds cliché, but it's true. When I'm dehydrated or exhausted, my skin shows it immediately. I also try to eat lots of healthy fats—avocados, salmon, nuts. Beauty really does start from the inside.

---

**Have your beauty philosophies changed as you've gotten older?**

Completely. In my twenties I was chasing trends and piling on product. Now I'm all about health and simplicity. I've stopped fearing aging—every line tells a story. My goal isn't to look twenty-five; it's to look like the healthiest, happiest version of myself at whatever age I am. That mindset shift changed everything.

**Final question—what's the one beauty product you'd never give up?**

Sunscreen, hands down. If I could go back and tell my younger self one thing, it would be to wear SPF every single day. It's the ultimate anti-aging secret, and it's not glamorous, but it works.

---

*Brooke Burns proves that true beauty isn't about the newest miracle product or a complicated regimen—it's about consistency, confidence, and knowing when to let your natural self shine through.*

# Real Talk: Ashley Chen on Beauty Bargains and Surviving Sophomore Year

*The rising star opens up about her go-to drugstore steals and the braces-and-bangs era she'd rather forget.*

---

**You've talked before about being a "beauty minimalist." What does that actually mean day-to-day?**

It means I'm cheap! [laughs] No, honestly, it means I've learned that expensive doesn't equal better. I spent years thinking I needed a $60 foundation to look put-together, and then a makeup artist on set handed me a drugstore concealer and it changed my whole routine. Now I'm that person clogging up the aisle at the pharmacy reading ingredient labels.

**Okay, we need the specifics. What's always in your bag?**

The e.l.f. Halo Glow Liquid Filter—it's their answer to a very famous expensive one, and I genuinely can't tell the difference. For mascara, I'll never quit the classic L'Oréal Voluminous. And CeraVe moisturizer, the one in the tub. I keep three tubs going at all times, which my boyfriend finds deeply annoying.

**Three tubs?**

Bathroom, nightstand, and one that lives in my car for some reason. Don't judge me.

**Any product that surprised you?**

Vaseline. Sounds so basic, but I put it on my lids for a dewy look and over lip color so it doesn't dry out. A makeup artist told me half of Hollywood does it. It costs, what, four dollars?

**Let's rewind. You've mentioned your high school years weren't exactly glamorous.**

Oh, they were a *situation.* I had this phase where I cut my own bangs—too short, obviously—and I was very committed to blue eyeshadow. Like, up to the eyebrow. Plus braces with the colored rubber bands. I'd change the colors for holidays. Very festive. Very unfortunate.

**Did you feel awkward at the time, or is it only funny in hindsight?**

Deeply awkward at the time. I was tall before everyone else, so I slouched constantly. I ate lunch in the library sometimes because I didn't know where to sit. I think a lot of people assume actresses were the popular ones, and I really want teenagers to know—I was not that girl. I was the one narrating a fantasy book series in my head during PE.

**How'd you get from there to here?**

Drama club, honestly. It was the first place the awkwardness became useful. Being a little weird, a little too much—suddenly that was an asset instead of something to hide. I found my people.

**What would you tell your sophomore-year self?**

Put down the bangs scissors. [laughs] But really—the stuff that made me feel like an outsider is the exact stuff people connect with now. Just hang in there and maybe blend your eyeshadow.

---

*Ashley Chen stars in the new series* Nightingale Court, *streaming this fall.*

# The Beauty Lesson That Started on a Ballet Barre

*How one performer's childhood in the wings shaped a lifelong relationship with makeup—and why she's still learning*

---

There's a particular smell that transports Elena Marchetti back to being seven years old: cold cream and hairspray, the perfume of backstage before a recital.

"My mother would sit me down on this wobbly stool," she recalls, laughing over an iced matcha at a quiet corner table. "And she'd tell me, 'Hold still, or you'll look like a raccoon who lost a fight.' That was my first makeup lesson. Very glamorous."

At 38, Marchetti has the kind of luminous, low-maintenance glow that entire industries have been built around promising. But she's quick to dismantle any assumption that it came naturally.

## The Ballerina Years

Long before red carpets, there was the recital circuit—and the surprisingly technical world of stage makeup for young dancers.

"When you're a child ballerina, makeup isn't about looking pretty. It's about being *seen*," she explains. "Stage lights wash you out completely. So you learn to draw yourself back in. My mother would give me these dramatic false lashes, and I felt like a tiny, terrifying swan."

She remembers the specific ritual: the bright blush swept high on the cheekbones, the eyeliner that seemed comically bold up close but read as subtle from the audience.

"I learned about the *distance* between how something looks in the mirror and how it looks in the world," she says. "That's stayed with me forever. Sometimes the boldest choice is the right one. Sometimes what feels like too much is exactly enough."

## What She Actually Uses

We asked her to walk us through her real routine—not the aspirational version.

**The base:** "A tinted moisturizer with SPF. I skipped sunscreen for years and I regret every single unprotected day."

**The cheeks:** A cream blush, applied with fingers. "My mother would be horrified. She was a brush purist. But I like the mess of it."

**The eyes:** Curled lashes, one coat of mascara. "The false lashes were retired with the pointe shoes."

**The finishing touch:** A lip balm with a hint of color. "I want to look like myself on a good day, not like a different person entirely."

## The Lesson That Lasted

What surprises her most, she says, is how much her mother's offhand backstage wisdom holds up.

"She used to say makeup was a costume you could take off, so there was no reason to be precious about it," Marchetti reflects. "You experiment, you make mistakes, you wash it off, you try again tomorrow. There's freedom in that."

She pauses, stirring her drink.

"I think a lot of people carry so much anxiety about their faces. But if you grow up seeing makeup as *play*—as this thing you do to tell a story under bright lights—it takes the weight off. It's just paint. You are already the whole ballet."

---

*Elena Marchetti's spring project is set to be announced later this year.*

---

*This article was produced in partnership with our beauty editorial team. Products mentioned were selected independently.*

# Backstage Beauty: A Chat with "Miss Guided" Star

*In this lighthearted sit-down, we caught up with one of the stars of the workplace comedy "Miss Guided" to dish about her everyday beauty essentials. Grab a coffee and settle in!*

---

**INTERVIEWER:** Thanks for taking the time to chat! Let's get right to the fun stuff. On busy filming days, what's the one product you absolutely cannot live without?

**ACTRESS:** Oh, that's easy—my eyeliner. I'm completely useless with a pencil, so I've become obsessed with a good liquid liner with a felt tip. It gives you that control without the shaky-hand disaster. I do a tiny flick at the corner and suddenly I feel like I have my life together, even if I've only had four hours of sleep!

**INTERVIEWER:** *(laughing)* The confidence of a good wing! Any tricks for beginners?

**ACTRESS:** Yes! Little dashes instead of one big swoop. Connect the dots afterward. Nobody needs to know it took three tries.

---

**INTERVIEWER:** Let's talk foundation. What's your philosophy?

**ACTRESS:** Less is more, honestly. Under those set lights, heavy foundation just melts right off. I go for something lightweight and buildable—a tinted moisturizer with a bit of coverage. I dab it on with a damp sponge so it really sinks into the skin instead of sitting on top. And I always, *always* moisturize first. Skincare before makeup is my whole religion.

---

**INTERVIEWER:** And the hair! It always looks so effortless. What's the secret?

**ACTRESS:** *(laughing)* "Effortless" is doing a lot of heavy lifting there! Honestly, my biggest secret is a good dry shampoo and not washing it every single day. It behaves so much better on day two. I also swear by a leave-in conditioner to fight the frizz, especially when we're shooting outdoors.

**INTERVIEWER:** Any final beauty wisdom for our readers?

**ACTRESS:** Drink your water, get your sleep, and don't take any of it too seriously. At the end of the day, the best beauty product is just having fun with it!

# The Beauty Edit: How This Actress Is Raising a Confident Daughter, One Skincare Ritual at a Time

*The star opens up about affordable beauty must-haves, the makeup lessons she's passing down, and why less is always more.*

---

There's a particular kind of magic that happens in a bathroom mirror on a weekday morning—the kind where a mother and daughter lean in close, sharing space and secrets. For this actress and single mom, those moments have become some of her most treasured.

"I never wanted beauty to feel like a mask for her," she says, settling into a chair with a cup of coffee, her face refreshingly bare. "I wanted it to feel like play. Like taking care of yourself, not covering yourself up."

## The Lessons That Matter

When it comes to what she's teaching her 13-year-old, the actress is intentional. The first rule? Skincare before makeup, always.

"I tell her all the time: your skin is the canvas, and you have to love the canvas first," she laughs. "We do our nightly routine together. It's become our thing—we talk about her day while we're washing our faces. Honestly, I get more out of her at the sink than I do at the dinner table."

Her second lesson is one she wishes she'd learned earlier: **you don't need much.**

"I grew up thinking more product equaled more beautiful. It took me years—and a lot of wasted money—to realize that a little concealer, some brow gel, and a good lip balm can do everything," she says. "I want her to start there. To understand that confidence isn't something you buy at the counter."

## Her Budget-Friendly Favorites

Contrary to what her red-carpet appearances might suggest, this actress is a devoted drugstore shopper—and proud of it.

"People assume because I'm in this industry that I'm using thousand-dollar creams. I'm really not," she insists. "Some of the best things I've ever used cost less than lunch."

Her non-negotiables include:

- **A gentle gel cleanser** ("Under fifteen dollars and it's never let me down. My daughter uses it too.")
- **A basic ceramide moisturizer** ("The drugstore ones are formulated by dermatologists. You're paying for the fancy jar, not better ingredients.")
- **Mineral sunscreen** ("This is the hill I will die on. I've been telling her since she was little—sunscreen is the best anti-aging product on the planet, and it's cheap.")
- **A multi-use balm** ("Lips, cuticles, dry patches, taming eyebrows. One tube does it all.")
- **Petroleum jelly for 'slugging'** ("An old trick my grandmother taught me. Costs almost nothing and my skin drinks it up overnight.")

## The Bigger Picture

Beyond the products, what she really hopes to hand down is something less tangible.

"There's so much pressure on girls right now, especially with everything they see online," she says, her tone softening. "I can't shield her from all of it. But I can show her a mom who looks in the mirror and likes what she sees. Who has crow's feet and laugh lines and doesn't panic about them."

She pauses. "I think the most important beauty advice I can give her isn't about a product at all. It's just: be kind to your face. Be kind to yourself. That's the whole secret."

As for whether her daughter actually *listens*?

"Some days, absolutely. Other days she rolls her eyes and steals my highlighter," she grins. "But that's the job, right? You plant the seeds and hope they grow."
